# Abstract

Each day, Nasdaq publishes auction imbalance information during the ten minutes leading up to the closing auction in order to attract liquidity and improve price discovery. In doing so it prints a mechanical signal that is learnable and strongly predictive of returns into the 16:00 close. We build a full trading system around this signal on the principles of classical statistical arbitrage: a forecast of 15:50 - 16:00 returns, a covariance estimate, and a model of trading costs, assembled as the terms of a single-period maximization problem which is solved for an optimal portfolio of dollar holdings. Our features are time-series and cross-sectional transformations of signed dollar imbalance. We model return forecasts by boosting a lasso regression with xgboost, which robustly achieves a 29% average rank information coefficient and MSE of $7e10^-6$ throughout cross-validation. We estimate risk with a rank-10 factor model of causally standardized returns, and we include spread costs and an Almgren-Chriss square-root instantaneous impact model. Backtested over 110 days, the strategy achieves a Sharpe ratio at capacity of 8.44. We argue that this elevated performance is expected given a high-IC forecast over a ten minute horizon, and that the real limits on the strategy are capacity and execution: GMV is constrained to below ~\$60M, and most of the forecasted return is realized within the first five milliseconds after the imbalance begins dissemination, making institutional grade execution and latency highly important in implementation. We believe that this strategy would see the most success if integrated into an optimal execution pipeline serving a larger statistical arbitrage portfolio, allowing for a small but persistent improvement while rebalancing large positions near the close.

# Motivation and Main Ideas {#sec-intro}

The Nasdaq equities closing auction occurs at 16:00:00 each trading day, and relavent auction imformation is published at a regular interval from 15:50:00 onward. At about 15:50:00, the exchange begins publishing information on the imbalance of auction orders. That is, the number of shares from on-close orders that will not be left over after matching the maximum number of shares at the calculated auction execution price, as well as the side (buy/sell/none) of the left over shares. The purpose of the auction imbalance publication is to attract auction liquitidy to the opposite side of the imbalance, maximizing the number of shares executed and providing the best possible end-of-day price discovery. Therefore, a thesis exists: auction imbalance published from 15:50:00 through the close provides a mechanical signal that is learnable and strongly predictive of returns over that horizon. We will refer throughout to *dollar imbalance*, calculated as the number of imbalance shares multiplied by the exchange-estimated auction execution price at 15:50:00, signed by the side of the imbalance shares. Dollar imbalance and its time-series and cross-sectional convolutions will be the basis of our return forecasts throughout.

# Methodological Choices and Innovations {#sec-methods}

This trading system is designed using optimal portfolio construction, the method underpinning classical statistical-arbitrage. Given a single "period" or "horizon", we forecast per-asset returns, estimate their variance and covariance, and estimate the costs of trading. We then assemble these pieces as the terms of a maximization problem and solve for the optimal portfolio of dollar holdings $p^* \in \mathbb{R}^n$ over our horizon. The reason we use this framework is that it allows for non-trivial risk and cost dynamics to be accounted for in maximizing pnl over a given time horizon, such as factor-neutrality and hedging, lasso-like cost penalties, and instananeous impact modeling. This problem is also DCP/SOCP, so it allows for free-access solvers such as Clarabel to efficiently solve. The decision to use a single horizon, rather than multiple, is discussed in @sec-single-vs-multi.

$$
\begin{split}
\max_p \quad &\underbrace{f \, p}_{\text{alpha}} - \underbrace{p^T \, \Sigma_r \, p}_{\text{risk}} - \underbrace{C(u)}_{\text{spread}} - \underbrace{I(u)}_{\text{impact}} \\ 
\text{s.t.} \quad & p \, L_{mkt} = 0 \\
                  & \sqrt{p^T \Sigma_r p} \leq \sigma_{\$}
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-simple-problem}

@eq-simple-problem is the maximization problem we solve each day, where $f \in  \mathbb{R}^n$ is a vector of return forecasts, $u = p - p_0, u \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the vector of trades to be made over the horizon, $\Sigma_r \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is a covariance matrix of returns, $C(u)$ is the cost of trading, and $I(u)$ is the instantaneous price impact our trades. We discuss each term of the maximization problem, as well as the constraints, in detail in @sec-forecasting through @sec-optimzation.

## Forecasting {#sec-forecasting}

### Features
<!-- Ridge vs Lasso vs Lasso + XGBoost (difficult to outperform the hero features) -->

The main inputs for our trading system is a forecast of returns from 15:50 to the 16:00 closing auction. Making use of the strength of this signal, we take a keep-it-simple approach to modeling. We use two core features, and each is a transformation of signed dollar imbalance. One is a time series feature, which provides information across days, and one is cross-sectional, giving us information across assets, within days.

Firstly, we call our time series feature the "signed imbalance ratio". This is simply the signed dollar imbalance divided by an exponentially weighted moving average of past daily dollar volume. Second, for our cross-sectional feature we rank dollar imbalance across stocks each day, and divide by the auction participation, or the total liquidity available as limit-on-close orders as of 15:50. This ranking is then normalized using @eq-norm to arrive at our "normalized rank imbalance" feature which is constrained to the range [-1,1].

$$
\text{{norm rank}} = \frac{rank - min}{2(max - min)} - 1
$$ {#eq-norm}

The combination of these features gives us a strong indication of the assets most likely to move each day. We also used the cross-sectionally demeaned return from 15:45 to 15:50 as a signal of how much of the imbalance-driven return may have been preempted just before the close which could possibly lower the forecast magnitude.

### Models

The best forecasting model we found was a lasso regression boosted using xgboost. We utilized this structure because our most powerful feature, the normalized rank imbalance, is inherently linear, however the other features introduce weaker but significant non-linearity.

Using our two core features, as well as the demeaned pre-emptive return and interaction terms, we trained a lasso model with $\lambda = 10^-4$. We then trained an xgboost model on the same features against the lasso regression's residuals and combined them to create a boosted linear model (@eq-model). Using kfold validation with 8 folds, this model achieved an average IC across folds of 29%. @fig-diagnostics shows near-heteroskedasticity and near-normally distributed residuals, a good indication of accuracy without overfitting.

$$
\begin{split}
\hat{\beta} = \min_{\beta} \quad &\frac{1}{2} |y - X \beta|_2^2 + | \lambda \beta |_1 \quad \text{(lasso problem)} \\ 
\hat{f} &= X \hat{\beta} - \text{xgboost}(X)
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-model}

![Residual Diagnostics](images/residual_diagnostics.png){#fig-diagnostics}

## Covariance Estimation {#sec-covariance}
<!-- Factor modeling, centering and volatility scaling -->

The covariance matrix $\Sigma_r$ is the sole way that the we represent the variance and covariance of different assets. The optimizer uses this information to both quantify the risk (variance) of holding a given asset, and to hedge positions against each other (covariance) and achieve factor neutralities.

We represent $\Sigma_r$ using a factor model of standardized returns. We first volatility-adjust the $T \times n$ returns matrix $X$ into $\tilde{X}$ using a causal EWMA volatility estimate (lagged one day for causality), and take the best rank-10 singular value decomposition $\tilde{X} \approx U_{10} S_{10} V_{10}^{T}$. Because $\tilde{X}$ is unitless, the resulting loadings and residual variances must be mapped back into return units before the optimizer can use them. We do this with $C = \mathrm{Diag}(\mathrm{std}(X))$, the diagonal matrix of per-asset sample return volatilities, at the final computation of $\Sigma_r$ using the unitless $\tilde{\Sigma}$ so that $\Sigma_r$ carries units of squared daily return. The full model is estimated on daily bars over 2023-06-01 to 2025-06-01, a window deliberately disjoint from the 2025-06-11 to 2026-06-11 period over which the forecast and backtest run, so the covariance is used strictly out of sample.

$$
\begin{split}
&C = \mathrm{Diag}(\mathrm{std}(X)) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}
\qquad
F = U_{10} \\
&L = S_{10} \, V_{10}^T
\qquad
D = Diag(var(\tilde{X} - F \, L)), \quad D \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} \\
\quad &\Rightarrow \Sigma_F = \frac{1}{n-1} F^T \, F \\
      &\Rightarrow \tilde{\Sigma} = L^T \, \Sigma_F \, L + D \\
      &\boxed{\Sigma_r = C^T \, \tilde{\Sigma} \, C}
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-covariance}

Compared with the sample covariance matrix $\Sigma$, using this factor model of returns increases accuracy and drastically reduces numerical issues in solving for $p^*$. Empirically, we have found that the condition number of sample covariance is on the order of $10^5$ and it is not positive semi-definite (PSD), while the factor-modeled $\Sigma_r$ has a condition number on the order of $10^2$, and is PSD. It also allows us to use factor neutrality constraints in the optimizer, discussed further in @sec-optimzation, which prevents accidental concetration of risk along any particular direction of return variance. Without this model, the optimizer would run into numerical issues solving, and the integrity of the solve would be questionable at best due to very small eigenvalues leading to unrealistic near-zero risk directions that the optimizer would leverage heavily.

## Price Impact Modeling {#sec-impact}
<!-- Reference bouchaud papers and square-root impact model, tried different parameter values from 0 to 1.
Instantaneous impact only. -->

We model price impact as a square root impact model, as in @eq-impact. Rather than fitting values for the impact parameter $\gamma_i$ per asset, we experimented with multiple values from the range [0, 1], anchored around $\gamma \approx 0.15$ estimated by Almgren, R., C. Thum, E. Hauptmann, and H. Li (2005) using institutional trading data from Citigroup. Since we are working on a ten minute horizon with one round-trip trade that is latency constrained, we assume that the only impact cost is instantaneous or temporary impact, modeled in @eq-impact.

$$
\underbrace{I_i}_{\text{return impact}} \;=\; \gamma_i \; \sigma_i \;
\sqrt{\dfrac{Q^{\$}_i}{\mathrm{ADV}^{\$}_i}}
$$ {#eq-impact}

## Optimizer {#sec-optimzation}
<!-- Single period MVO + spread cost + instantaneous impact. -->

As mentioned in @sec-methods, we make use of classical statistical arbitrage machinery to estimate the optimal dollar holdings over our trading horizon. The full maximization problem is stated in @eq-full-problem. We use a single-period MVO along with spread cost and instantaneous impact terms, and use CVXPY to independently solve for the optimal dollar portfolio over each period. At each period we solve the below problem.
$$
\begin{split}
\max_p \quad &f \, p - p^T \, \Sigma_r \, p - \frac{s}{2} |p| - \dfrac{|p|^{3/2}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{ADV}}} \\ 
\text{s.t.} \quad & p \, L_{mkt} = 0 \\
                  & \sqrt{p^T \Sigma_r p} \leq \sigma_{\$}
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-full-problem}

We also subject our optimal portfolio to factor neutral constraints, specifically neutrality against the factor of largest variance (the market factor) derived from the earlier SVD, and to expected dollar volatility constraints. This strategy is less sensitive to volatility than to costs and impact, since this is a relatively fast strategy with high feature ICs, however the factor neutrality guarantee enforces a reliance only on forecasted returns, not market movements generally. The expected dollar volatility ensures that the portfolio is never expected to move by more than some cap, which helps control risk and prevents the optimizer from suggesting a rapid increase in GMV.

# Empirical Results {#sec-findings}

## Backtest {#sec-backtest}
<!-- Really really good backtest. Every thing seems real. -->
We conduct our backtest over 110 days from [2026-01-01, 2026-06-11], adn we attempt to get a best estimate of the sharpe ratio of this strategy at its full-capacity GMV limit. Recall from @sec-data that the forecasting model was trained on [2025-06-11, 2025-12-31] and the covariance model on daily data from [2023-06-01, 2026-01-01]. The annualized sharpe ratio over this backtest was ~8.44. The mean GMV was $53M and maximum was $60M, with total net pnl of $2.8M and maximum expected volatility fo $1M. Testing GMVs above this maximum of ~$60M leads to diminishing returns in PNL. The parameters for this run are in @tbl-params and results in @tbl-results, the daily dollar portfolio weights are in @fig-weights, and the results are in @fig-backtest.

| Parameter | Value | Desc. |
|-----------|:------|:------:|
| Lambda      | 1e-8  |Risk param. on the order of ~ 1 / GMV|
| Gamma       | 0.15  |Impact param. ranging from [0, 1].   |
| exp_vol_cap | $1e6   |Expected portfolio volatility cap.   |
: Backtest Parameters {#tbl-params}

At these and similar parameter values, the optimizer produces relatively stable performance and gross market-value (GMV). It has very slight drawdowns and very high sharpe, with small but consistent gains. Although this may ring alarm bells, it is to be expected with this type of alpha and will be furthur discussed in @sec-capacity.

## Capacity and Execution Constraints {#sec-capacity}
<!-- This is constrained to max capacity under $100M, likely $40-60M GMV, with peak returns reached much earlier. This is due to the short horizon constraining the ability to chunk orders, and the latency requirements of the signal, and the relatively small size of auction imbalances.

This would require exceptional execution quality and speed, as most of the forecasted return happens in the first 250ms after the imbalance is first printed by the exchange. -->
This strategy's performance in @sec-backtest is phenomenal, and may seem overstated of raise alarm of bias or error. However, this level of performance is to be expected in such a strategy using high IC features over a short horizon. The crucial thing is that this alpha is subject to serious capacity and execution constraints.

Firstly, given the short timeframe of trading, the capacity of this alpha is constrained to GMVs below ~$80M. Since we are effectively dumping the entire capacity into and out of the market at one instant around 15:50 and the close auction, we have high instantaneous impact. The nature of our exit strategy also being MOC orders opposite to the auction imbalance means that our trading reduces the affect of the imbalance on price, so we are doubly constrained. 

Given the high price impact, we may be inclined to spread out trades over the ten minute window, however, two things prevent this. First, NASDAQ only accepts MOC orders until 15:55, so the exit MOC orders must be placed before then, restricting us to five minutes of trading. More importantly though, @fig-markout shows about 30% of the forecasted return from 15:50 - close is realized within the first 100us after Nasdaq first disseminates the auction imbalance, and 60% within the first 5ms. This means that the strategy is stuck with high price impact and that institutional grade execution quality and latency is a prerequisite. This also means that in practice, the staggered nature of live messages leads to the risk that early arrivals' forecasted returns become realized before the entire universe has reported feature values.

![Returns Markout over Forecast Horizon Bucketed by Feature Quintiles](images/markout.png){#fig-markout}


# Future Work {#sec-future}

<!-- Future work would include improving the forecast as well as studying overnight signals. Possibly adding a second period from 15:55-15:58 when continuous and LOC orders are accepted. Improving impact estimation. Developing an execution simulator to test for implementation shortfall and more exact latency requirements. -->

The main areas for further research in this strategy are, as always, improving current forecasts and adding new ones. Most important would be adding a forecast of overnight returns. A likely first-pass improvement would be modeling the reversion of close auction returns into the next-day open. This would improve the strategy's capacity and pnl by lengthening the alpha's horizon and allowing for better management of price impact. This would also necessitate overnight volatility modeling.

As it stands, this system is a high-sharpe, low-capacity opportunity. We believe that it would likely achieve the most success as part of an optimal execution pipeline within a larger, longer horizon statistical arbitrage system. This way, the relatively small but consistent alpha demonstrated here can be captured while rebalancing larger positions near the closing auction.

# Appendix {#sec-appendix}

## Data {#sec-data}
<!-- Databento imbalance, tbbo, and statistics (official auction) from XNAS.ITCH. -->

Throughout this work we use a combination of [daily statistics](https://databento.com/docs/schemas-and-data-formats/statistics?historical=python&live=python&reference=python), [trades and BBO](https://databento.com/docs/schemas-and-data-formats/tbbo?historical=python&live=python&reference=python), and [imbalance](https://databento.com/docs/schemas-and-data-formats/imbalance?historical=python&live=python&reference=python) data. All data used here is sourced through [Databento](https://databento.com/docs/schemas-and-data-formats/mbp-10?historical=python&live=python&reference=python), and their XNAS.ITCH dataset. The exception to this is expensive corporate-action adjustment factors which are sourced via yfinance and sometimes inferred via Databento's daily data. 

We chose to use one year of trades, BBO, and imbalance data from 2025-06-11 through 2026-06-11 in order to minimize expense and memory complexity. We split into train [2025-06-11, 2025-12-31], and test [2026-06-01, 2026-06-11] ranges and also use CAX-adjusted daily data from [2023-06-01, 2026-01-01] for the covariance modeling. The train/test split allowed us to avoid the difficult machinery of rolling-universe selection and instead use a single static universe of the 50 - 500 highest ADV Nasdaq equities from the train set.

## Single vs Multi Period Optimization {#sec-single-vs-multi}
<!-- 10 minute signal, only one forecast, rebalancing would cost more than it's worth. -->
The decision to use a "myopic" single period optimizer instead of optimizing over a multi-period position path was driven by the nature of the alpha forecast we are using. The horizon being only 10mins means we have very little opportunity to trade and that our forecasts are more accurate but also smaller than daily forecasts. In turn, this means we have few opportunities to trade and frequent rebalancing costs more than it is worth. If overnight forecasts are later developed (see @sec-future) we would recommend moving toward multi-period planning to reduce price impact.
